At the edge of the garden, where the fence gives up and the grass grows wild, there’s a small patch of mint.

Nobody planted it there. It arrived on its own, or so the gardener says. Every summer it spreads a little farther, bright and unruly, smelling like cold water and clean beginnings. You can pull it up by the handful, but it always comes back.

I like that about mint. It doesn’t ask whether the garden has room. It doesn’t wait for permission. It finds a crack in the hard ground and makes something green.

Somewhere, right now, a seed is doing the same: no map, no promise, just a small insistence on becoming.
